newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK pro-democracy groups step up leadership protest.
newsitem.headline: HK pro-democracy groups step up leadership protest.

text.p: Vocal sections of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement said on Friday they would step up their protest against China's methods of picking the territory's future leaders.
The Frontier, a pressure group led by pro-democracy legislators, said it would stage a two-month campaign against the process which it called unrepresentative and elitist.

The group plans to stage street dramas and public rallies, hand out leaflets and place advertisements in newspapers to protest against the way a China-selected electoral college will choose the leaders to take over after the handover next year.

"We want to let people know that it is not the case that everyone in Hong Kong can participate in the election," Frontier co-founder Lee Cheuk-yan told Reuters. "We are only bystanders in the process."

Another group comprising a loose coalition of small pro-democracy pressure groups said it would submit a blank nomination form to the electoral college that China is setting up in Hong Kong. Spokesman Chan Kwok-leung said the action would symbolise their outrage over the "small circle" selection process.

China has promised Hong Kong considerable autonomy in running its affairs when a century and a half of British rule ends at midnight on June 30, 1997. Hong Kong citizens, not Chinese cadres, will lead the territory of 6.2 million people who have been assured they can retain their capitalist way of life.

The China-appointed Preparatory Committee, responsible for transforming Hong Kong from a British colony to a Special Administrative Region of China, has determined that the post-colonial leadership will be named by a 400-strong electoral college called the Selection Committee.

The month-long nomination process to the Selection Committee, responsible for naming both a chief executive and a controversial Provisional Legislature, ends on Saturday. More than 3,200 names have been put forward but it remains to be seen precisely how the 400 candidates will be chosen or how they in turn will choose Hong Kong's post-colonial leaders.
The Chief Executive-designate, who will replace colonial Governor Chris Patten, is expected to be named by November to give him or her time to prepare for power.

The selection process has been fraught with controversy and political quarrels over the legitimacy of China's plan to scrap the elected Legislative Council and replace it with a provisional legislature after the handover.
On Thursday, senior Hong Kong civil servants lost a legal battle to reverse a ban on them standing for the Selection Committee.
The Hong Kong government maintains the ban is necessary in order to preserve the neutrality of the civil service.
